In Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), a frozen reference model is one that remains unchanged after initial training to provide consistent feedback for subsequent refinements of the AI's performance. This approach contrasts with dynamic models where adjustments can be made during interaction based on human feedback.

In Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), a frozen reference model is used to pre-train an AI system on a large dataset of human interactions. Once trained, this model retains its learned behavior but can be easily modified or replaced with another version that adapts to specific tasks or user preferences during the final fine-tuning phase for reinforcement learning. This approach allows for continuous improvement and adaptation without requiring extensive retraining each time new feedback is received.

In Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), a frozen reference model refers to an AI system that uses the output of another AI system as its initial state or input for training itself. This allows human feedback to be incorporated into the learning process without requiring extensive data collection and annotation efforts from humans. The frozen reference model acts as a "teacher" that guides the learning of the reinforcement learning algorithm, ensuring it adapts more quickly and effectively to complex tasks based on real user interactions.

In Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), a frozen reference model refers to the process where the AI system uses a pre-trained human-in-the-loop agent as an initial starting point for learning new skills or improving performance. This approach allows the AI to benefit from the learned behaviors and knowledge of a skilled human, potentially speeding up training and enhancing the overall quality of reinforcement learning outcomes.

In Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), a frozen reference model is one that remains unchanged throughout the training process, only receiving feedback from human annotators to refine its policies or parameters. This approach helps maintain consistency and avoids the complexity of adapting an evolving model to new data over time.
